title: Flip Even-Sized Groups in a Chain
statement:
You get the head of a linked list. Cut it, from the front, into consecutive groups of sizes 1, 2, 3, 4, … . The last group gets whatever nodes are left, so it may be shorter than its planned size.

Reverse the order of nodes inside every group whose actual length is even. Leave the other groups as they are. Return the head of the resulting list.

examples.why: Groups: [5], [2, 8], [1, 7, 3], [9, 4, 6]. The last group was meant to hold 4 nodes but only 3 are left, so it is odd and stays. Only [2, 8] flips.
Groups: [1], [2, 3], [4, 5, 6], [7, 8]. The last group was meant to hold 4 but has 2 nodes, which is still even, so it flips.
The second group was meant to hold 2 nodes but only has 1. Its actual length is odd, so nothing changes.

hints: Before deciding whether to reverse a group, you need its real length. How do you find it without walking past the end?
Keep a pointer to the node just before the current group. Walk ahead up to `size` nodes to count the group.
If the count is even, reverse exactly that many nodes after the pointer and reconnect both ends; the old first node becomes the new pointer. Otherwise just step the pointer forward by the count.

explain.intuition:
Each group is a slice of the list, and the rule depends on the slice's actual length, not its planned size. So for every group, first count how many nodes it really has (stop at size or at the end), then decide.

Reversing a slice in place is the usual three-pointer reversal, with two extra links to fix: the node before the slice must point at the new first node, and the old first node (now last) must point at whatever follows the slice. Keeping a pointer to "the node before the current group" makes both easy. The first group always has length 1, so it never flips, and its single node is a natural starting point for that pointer.
steps: Set prev = head (the first group is just the head) and size = 2.
While prev.next exists, walk forward from prev.next up to size nodes, counting len and stopping at the node after the group.
If len is even, reverse those len nodes so the old first node points at after, set prev.next to the new first node, and move prev to the old first node.
If len is odd, advance prev by len nodes.
pitfalls: Deciding by the planned size: a final group meant to hold 4 that only has 3 nodes must not flip, and one meant to hold 3 that has 2 must.
Forgetting to link the reversed group's new tail to the rest of the list, which cuts the list off.
Advancing prev to the new group head after reversing instead of to the old first node, which is now the group's last node.

solutions.title: Copy values to an array
solutions.idea: Read all values into an array, reverse the right slices there, and write the values back into the nodes.

solutions.title: Reverse groups in place
solutions.idea: Keep the node before each group; count the group, then reverse it with pointer surgery when its length is even.

followups: Reverse the odd-length groups instead. What changes about the first group?
Group sizes follow another sequence, for example powers of two. Which part of the code depends on the sizes?
